1:
Ellicott notes that this is one of the few parables introduced by a distinct statement of its drift and aim. Henry says the same in a figure, that the parable has its key hanging at the door. They differ on how wide the drift runs. Lightfoot keeps the thread from the previous chapter, where the coming of Christ to avenge himself on Jerusalem was in view, and reads not to faint against the afflictions they were to meet; Clarke and Gill agree, pointing to the desolations coming on the land as the reason for being instant in prayer. Theophylact makes the connection from the other end, that having spoken of the trials at hand our Lord adds their remedy at once, constant and earnest prayer. Wesley widens it again, taking this parable and the next as warnings against two fatal extremes, faintness and self-confidence.

What the perseverance amounts to is then defined. Calvin calls it a rare and difficult attainment, and finds a mark of unbelief in the way we throw away hope and all the ardour of prayer when the first attempt fails; the comparison used here, harsh as it looks, teaches importunity until we draw from God what he seems unwilling to give, though not because prayer wins a victory over him or bends him slowly to compassion, but because his listening is not at once evident. Barnes divides the word always into four duties: not neglecting stated seasons, seizing on remarkable providences, keeping a praying frame at all times, and not wearying when prayer seems unanswered. Robertson takes the second verb literally, not to give in to evil, that is, to turn coward and lose heart.

The older readings press the argument from the lesser to the greater. Augustine puts it plainly: if with the most unjust of judges the suppliant's perseverance at last prevailed, how much more confidently may those pray who never cease asking of God, the fountain of justice and mercy. Tertullian uses the parable polemically, insisting that the judge to be importuned is God himself, and arguing that because the one who judges is also the avenger of his own elect, the Creator is on that account the specially good God. Bede takes up the closing question about faith on earth, holding that the elect will be so scarce at the end that it is less the cries of the faithful than the torpor of the rest which hastens the world's fall, and that our Lord speaks as though in doubt not because he doubts but to reprove us.

The two figures are then set out. Gill describes the courts an Israelite city would have had, the great council of seventy-one at Jerusalem, a lesser of twenty-three where there were six score men, and three judges where fewer. Ellicott reads the case historically, as testimony to the corruption of justice under the government then ruling Galilee and Peraea, and adds that it is deliberately extreme, conscience being dead and no love of approbation left to supply its place. Clarke says no man is worthy of so sacred an office who does not deeply fear God and tenderly respect his fellow creatures, and notes that even among the heathen this described a man wholly abandoned, citing a historian's verdict on an emperor. Barnes draws the halves together, that one with no regard for God may be expected to have none for man, so the description teaches indirectly what a judge ought to be; Robertson calls him a judge who acknowledged no superior. On the widow's plea Clarke and Barnes both correct the English, which should read that she asked justice against her adversary rather than vengeance; Clarke adds that a suitor seeking revenge would never have been given a place in the record. Ellicott notices that the tense implies continual coming, and that the law's delay was worse to her than the original wrong.
4:
The judge's motive is examined more closely than his act. Barnes points out that he took up the case not from regard to justice or his office but simply to avoid trouble, though his conduct might for all that have looked upright and even strictly legal. Clarke complains likewise that many actions which look good have neither the love of God nor of our neighbour behind them, but only self-love of the basest kind. Ellicott adds a harder touch: the man had passed beyond hypocrisy and saw himself as others saw him, and as God saw him.

What finally moves him is put in the language of the ring. Clarke renders the verb as stun me and traces it to boxers who blacken the eyes by beating about the face. Ellicott works the word out further, since it appears elsewhere for keeping the body under, and thinks it passed from the arena into ordinary speech much as we now talk of landing a knock-down blow in debate, what is described being a continuous shower of such blows. Robertson reports that some take the judge to be literally afraid of being struck under the eye, and sets it aside, since that sense would have called for a different tense.

The argument from the lesser to the greater is stated and then guarded. Clarke draws it out: if a man of such character could yield to a poor widow he felt nothing but contempt for, how much more ready must God be, who is infinitely good and loves his creatures tenderly. Ellicott admits that the choice jars, an extreme instance of human unrighteousness being made the parable of prayer, and finds only partial relief in the comparison, that if repeated entreaties prevail with men whose will is set against the suppliant, they prevail far more with God, in whom will anticipates the prayer. Barnes states the principle that resolves it, that the character of God is not represented by this judge at all, many circumstances in a parable being mere appendages to the narrative and not to be interpreted closely. Calvin says the same, that in applying the parable Christ does not make God resemble a wicked judge but points to a different reason why believers are kept long in suspense.

On the delay they divide. Lightfoot takes the long-suffering here and a like phrase in an epistle to concern the same thing, the destruction of Jerusalem and the years before it, when the Lord bore with his elect in a slippery time when apostasy prevailed and men were as hard to keep as to gain. Gill dates the vindication to the few years after Christ's death, when the elect among the Jews were delivered while the Roman army made havoc of their enemies, and only then extends it to the end of the world; Wesley reads it the same way. Robertson makes the delay patient forbearance, not indifference; Barnes locates the real danger not in God's faithfulness but in his afflicted people losing heart. Calvin describes the offence to be met, since we daily see treachery and cruelty abounding, no regard to justice and no shame, the poor groaning under their oppressors and the innocent insulted, while God appears asleep in heaven, so that the flesh concludes the world is governed by a blind fortune. The last question divides them further. Clarke will not read it of the world at all, rendering it whether fidelity shall be found in this land, whether the soil has borne a harvest proportioned to its culture, and answering no, which is why that land was destroyed. Ellicott takes it of the Church's history and every day of the Lord preluding the final Advent, Wesley of how few true believers will be found on earth whenever he appears. Robertson will not settle whether the sentence is a question, though he thinks on the whole it is.
9:
The target of the second parable is stated as plainly as the first. Augustine gives the link: since faith is the gift not of the proud but of the humble, a parable about humility and against pride follows at once. Henry divides the fault in two, a great conceit of their own goodness which reckoned them holier than their neighbours, and a confidence before God which pleaded the merit of it, as though they had made him their debtor. Barnes says they trusted to their own works rather than to God and counted everyone else a sinner, which he makes the standing character of self-righteousness. Clarke translates the verb as disdained, made nothing of, treated with contempt, and grants that these men made the outside clean while asking what was lodged within. Ellicott is less sure the hearers were Pharisees at all: they are not so named, and he thinks disciples in whom the Pharisee temper was gaining ground were included, to be taught by an argument carried to absurdity. Gill puts the aim simply, to expose their arrogance; Calvin generalises it, no disease being more dangerous than arrogance or so deeply fixed in the marrow of the bones.

Whether the man was a hypocrite is quietly disputed. Wesley denies it outright: the parable was not spoken to hypocrites, and this Pharisee was no more one than an outward adulterer is, since he sincerely trusted that he was righteous and told God so in a prayer none but God heard. Robertson reaches nearly the opposite conclusion from the grammar, since the man stood so as to be seen and prayed with himself, which makes the whole a soliloquy and a complacent recital of his own virtues rather than fellowship with God, the thanks being for those virtues and not for any mercy received. He adds that a rabbinic prayer survives in the same shape, thanking God that the speaker was a Jew and not a Gentile, a Pharisee and not one of the common people.

The fathers dwell on the shape of the pride rather than its object. Theophylact notices the order of the prayer, that the man begins with what he had not and only then names what he had. Chrysostom presses the second half: to despise the whole race was not enough for him, he must attack the publican too, and would have sinned far less had he spared him, since in one word he assails the absent and wounds the man present. Giving thanks, he says, is not heaping reproaches on others; when a man returns thanks let God be all in all to him. Bede reads the pair typically, the Pharisee for the Jewish people who boast of the righteousness of the law and the publican for the Gentiles who, being far from God, confess their sins, so that the one went home humbled and the other was counted worthy to draw near.

The scene itself is filled in by two of them. Ellicott observes that going up is strictly accurate, the temple standing high above the city, and that the two names would have been far more vivid to the first hearers, the one figure marked by the broad fringe and the phylacteries on brow and shoulder, the other in working dress with no badge of the covenant; he adds that the parable may be relating actual facts. Gill notes the Jewish conviction that prayer offered in the temple or a synagogue was more acceptable and sooner heard than prayer in private. Calvin sets the two side by side and marks how unlike they are for all the appearance of a common ardour, the one approaching with a commendation pronounced on his whole life as though entitled to offer the sacrifice of praise, the other as an outcast, with trembling and humble confession.
11:
The posture is argued about first. Clarke takes the phrase to mean that the man stood by himself, thinking it disgraceful to appear connected with the penitent beside him, and prayed apart as well as stood apart, joining him neither in person nor in petition. Barnes reports the same rendering as apt to a sect that dreaded contact as polluting and was for ever telling men to stand by themselves, but doubts whether the Greek will bear it. Ellicott objects that a false stress has been laid on the attitude, as though standing erect were itself a mark of pride, when the publican also stood and standing was the customary Jewish posture. Gill agrees that standing was a praying posture and nothing amiss, leaving open whether the man chose a place of eminence, a solemn attitude, or simply confidence. Calvin looks past the posture: the fault is not a boast of free will, since the thanksgiving does acknowledge what he had as God's gift, but a trust that God was reconciled to him by the merit of his works.

On the fasting the accounts do not agree: Barnes puts it on the second and fifth days of every week and Wesley on Monday and Thursday, which comes to the same thing, while Ellicott makes it the third and fifth. Robertson supplies the measure of the excess, that the law required one fast a year and the Pharisees added two a week over two seasons. Barnes adds that the surplus was made more meritorious because voluntary, and Calvin that the claim amounts to performing more than the law required, in the manner of those who talk loftily of works beyond obligation. Gill disposes of a rendering that would put the fast on the sabbath, a feasting day on which even the poorest man maintained by alms was bound to three meals, and fasting before noon forbidden. Lightfoot supplies the background, that fasts were of two kinds, of the congregation and of the single person, both chiefly for afflictions, the public sort answering to siege and pestilence and locust and drought, the private to a man's own trouble when someone belonging to him was sick or imprisoned or lost in the wilderness.

On the tithe the correction is unanimous. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all render the verb of acquiring rather than possessing, so the boast concerns income and not property. Ellicott adds that tithe was a tax on produce, and that the boast is of paying the lesser tithes as well as the greater. Clarke draws a rule from it, that a man who sets apart part of his earnings should never let it lie in his own hands, lest possession breed covetousness. Wesley reports that many gave a full tenth in tithes and a second tenth in alms, and reduces the whole plea to three clauses: I do no harm, I use all the means of grace, I do all the good I can.

Calvin allows that each of us is the more bound to thank the author of whatever virtues we have, and that pondering benefits received is a holy exercise, so the fault lies not in the thanksgiving but in swelling with confidence and preferring oneself to others. Ellicott makes the most surprising concession, setting this self-analysis beside the thanksgivings of a Stoic emperor and owning that the pagan's, though less systematic, is framed on a higher ethical standard. Clarke recalls that a righteousness exceeding this was made the condition of entering the kingdom.
13:
How far off the man stood, and from what, is not agreed. Barnes measures it from the sanctuary: prayer was offered in the court of the women, and while the Pharisee advanced to the side nearest the temple, this man stood at the other side of it, or in the court of the Gentiles if he was not a Jew, as far from the holy place as he could get. Wesley says the same, that the distance was from the holy of holies. Robertson denies it outright, holding that the distance was from the Pharisee and not from the sanctuary. Ellicott makes the motive shame, which kept him from the crowd pressing forward and above all from the respectable man beside him, as a forlorn castaway might crouch in the far corner of a cathedral nave; he adds that this man stood too, kneeling there being itself ostentatious. Clarke rules out one explanation, that he kept back as a heathen who dared not approach, since he was most likely a Jew, and puts it down to true penitence. Lightfoot supplies the topography, that Israelites at private prayer went past the outer court into the court of the women, as the thirteen alms chests there and the widow's two mites show, and doubts whether a private worshipper might come further in.

The downcast eyes are read for what they signify rather than prescribed. Clarke lists three things in the posture, deep distress, a conscious confession of guilt, and the very attitude the rabbins required. Robertson notes that worshippers commonly lifted their eyes to God, and that the smiting of the breast is in a tense of continued beating. Calvin warns against turning the description into a rule, since Christ did not mean that we must always cast our eyes down when we pray but was describing the tokens of humility, which lies in not refusing to acknowledge our sins but condemning ourselves and so anticipating the judgment of God. Wesley marks the feeling exactly, that the man was touched with shame, which he calls more ingenuous than fear.

The verdict is then pressed hard on one point. Calvin insists that the comparison is not one of degree, as though justification belonged to both men in different measures; the one was accepted and the other totally rejected. He uses the verse to fix the strict sense of the word, to stand before God as if we were righteous: the man was justified not by acquiring some new quality but by obtaining grace, his guilt blotted out and his sins washed away, from which it follows that justification consists in the forgiveness of sins. Clarke and Wesley reach the same in a clause each, Clarke that the other was simply not accepted, Wesley that the phrase means the one and not the other. Barnes puts it as a reversal of judgment, since the Pharisees would have said the first man was approved and are here assured that they judge wrongly.

Two further observations close the parable. Ellicott notices that the participle is perfect, implying a justification completed and abiding, and fastens on a word nobody else remarks: the house is made the test in both cases, home life trying whether worship was real, so that the one man's self-congratulation betrayed a conscience ill at ease in irritability and harshness, while the other went home, not in spite of his self-condemnation but because of it, with a new peace showing itself in gentleness. Robertson observes that the closing maxim had been used earlier in the Gospel, and quotes the fair question why it should be assumed that Jesus did not repeat his sayings. Gill only marks the contrast that carries the whole, that the man who freely owned himself a sinner was the one treated with contempt.
15:
Henry fits the incident to what precedes, as a confirmation of the parable just told, that those are accepted who humble themselves; and he turns it into a duty, that people blessed in Christ should want their children blessed in him too, which honours Christ and shows a real love of the children by a concern for their souls. Theophylact reads it as a lesson in humility taught by example, since our Lord does not turn the little ones away but receives them graciously. Ambrose is unwilling to think ill of the disciples for the rebuke, and offers two explanations: either they acted from a holy zeal that their Master should not be pressed by the crowds, and not from envy or hardness, or else the mystery is that they wished the Jewish people, whose kinsmen they were, to be saved first. He states the principle behind the charitable reading, that our own interest must be given up where an injury is threatened to God.

How old the children were, and whom Christ called, are the two questions that divide them. Gill argues from the grammar that the summons went to the children themselves, since no other antecedent is possible, and infers that they cannot have been new-born babes or children at the breast but were grown enough to be called and to come. Wesley says flatly that those called were the people who had brought them. Robertson takes both, having Christ call the children with their parents and then rebuke the disciples for their rebuke; but on the age he stands against Gill, noting that the word Luke uses is the old term for infants where the other Gospels have little children, and Henry agrees, describing them as too young to walk. Robertson adds two smaller marks of Luke's own hand, the also that the other accounts lack, and the tense of the rebuking, which is either a beginning or a continuing rather than a single act.

The background supplied is Jewish in one case and modern in another. Lightfoot reports the rabbinic dispute over the age at which a child becomes capable of the world to come, one authority dating it from birth, another from the time he can speak, another from conception, another from circumcision, and another from the time he can answer Amen; and he thinks it likely the apostles had taken up some such opinion. Clarke reaches for a living parallel, describing how a disciple brings his child to a spiritual teacher, presses the child's head down to his feet and receives a blessing in the form of wishes for long life, learning and wealth. Ellicott draws a conclusion of another kind from the wording, that the close agreement with the second Gospel through these two verses makes it likely that Luke had this passage from personal communication with its author.

What the child is held up for is stated most carefully by Robertson, who insists that the child is made the model for those seeking entrance into the kingdom and not the adult the model for the child, and that nothing here says the child is already in the kingdom without coming to Christ; he adds that the plea for children to be allowed to come is one many parents need to heed, since it is a tragedy when either parents or preachers become the obstacle. Wesley reads the saying as identifying the subjects of the Messiah's kingdom, to whom it properly belongs. Gill takes the following verse as the occasion for teaching the disciples humility and guarding them against pride and vanity, and Barnes lets the passage rest on the parallels and the psalm about the weaned child.
18:
Bede supplies the link with what precedes, that a ruler who had just heard only the childlike would enter the kingdom asks to be told plainly, and not in parable, by what works he might merit eternal life. Gill fills in the man, young, a magistrate and very rich, who ran after Jesus and overtook him on the road towards Jericho; Henry finds the sight a blessed one, since few rulers had any esteem for Christ and here was one who distinguished himself from his rank by a concern about his soul. Robertson notes that the title of ruler is peculiar to this Gospel, that the question asks by doing what he shall inherit, exactly as an earlier questioner framed it, and that the man seems to have supposed a single act would secure it; he also reports that no Jewish teacher was addressed as good. Titus of Bostra paraphrases the approach generously: I am learned in the older Scriptures but see in you something more excellent, since you make no earthly promises but preach the kingdom of heaven. Chrysostom will call the man covetous, because that is the reproach Christ brings, but refuses to call him a tempter. Lightfoot goes further and holds that he acknowledged Jesus as the Messiah, since others not yet disciples did so, and sees no reason to deny it of a man of such evident parts.

The reply sends him to the commandments, and the order they come in is noticed. Titus of Bostra reads the move as instruction in faith first, as though it were said, know God first and then it will be time to ask what you ask. Theophylact explains the sequence by what men are most prone to, adultery because the incitement is within us, murder because rage is a great and savage monster, and the sin against parents last because, grave as it is, it very seldom happens. Gill counts them, five only and not in their scriptural order, and takes the point to be that the law must be kept or satisfaction made before there can be any inheriting of life. Barnes contents himself with the texts of the decalogue, and Clarke refers the reader to his fuller handling of the case in the first Gospel.

Ellicott traces the account against the other two throughout: the first answer agrees more closely with the second Gospel, the omission of one clause from the commandments follows the first against the second, keeping them from youth up is shared with the second, as is the dropping of the question what more is lacking, the omission of taking up the cross follows the first again, and the word for the man's sorrow stands half-way between merely sorrowing and lowering. He adds that the adjective for his wealth is the very one used of the rich man in the earlier parable, which he finds suggestive.

On the demand itself the readings pull apart. Athanasius makes renunciation cost nothing, the whole earth beside heaven being but a span long, so that men who gave up the lordship of it all would have resigned nothing worth naming. Wesley draws the opposite line: the command was to cure a love of the world which in this man could be cured no other way, our Saviour knowing his heart and putting him on a trial that laid it open to himself; but he does not command us to sell all, only to use all to the glory of God. Robertson calls the words an amazing compliment to a man aiming at perfection, and thinks the youth had real charm and was sincere in his claims. Cyril describes the collapse in a figure, that he could not contain the new word but burst with sorrow like an old bottle.
24:
Theophylact reads the first saying carefully and notices that it stops short of impossibility: it is hard, not impossible, for the rich to enter, since they might after all reap a heavenly reward through their riches, though riches are more tenacious than birdlime and a soul once seized by them is hardly plucked away. He then observes that the next words do speak of it as impossible. Robertson agrees that the second saying names the impossible, calling the figure a current proverb for it and reporting that the Talmud twice puts an elephant through a needle's eye to the same effect. Gill supplies the occasion, that Christ saw by the man's looks that he was determined not to part with his possessions. Clarke records a textual curiosity instead, that a few manuscripts read a cable in place of the camel.

Ellicott follows the wording for what it shows about the writer. The word for needle here is not the one the other two Gospels use but a more classical term, theirs being unknown to Attic writers, and he counts the small fact among the signs of this evangelist's culture. He makes two further observations of the same kind: that the way the astonished question is introduced suggests either that others were present besides the disciples named elsewhere or that only some of them heard, and that the answer about the impossible takes here rather more the shape of a general axiom. Robertson explains why the question was astonishing at all, since wealth was assumed to be a mark of divine favour and not a hindrance to salvation, and he presses the answer as a paradox that holds: stand beside God and the impossible becomes possible, for God can break the grip of gold on a man's life, though even Christ did not break it here.

Peter's claim is handled gently. Robertson renders the words as our own things, meaning home and business, remarks that this is exactly where so many fail, and reports the judgment that Peter spoke not in boastfulness but out of the consternation the whole scene had produced. Clarke fills the phrase out as trades and houses and families. Cyril states the logic that makes the question fair: a rich man who has given up much will naturally look for a reward, but the man who had little and resigned what he had may reasonably ask what is in store for him. Ellicott finds something characteristic in what this Gospel leaves out of the list, since the lands named elsewhere are missing here, and suggests that a companion of Paul and Barnabas, to whom parting with a field was a small thing, might not have retained the word as marking any extraordinary sacrifice, whereas leaving a house meant breaking up a home.

What the hundredfold in this present time amounts to is the last question, and two answers stand against each other. Bede takes it of the man who in seeking the kingdom has despised all earthly affections and trampled on the riches and pleasures and smiles of the world, and reports that some build on this very declaration the fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the just, when everything surrendered for God's sake is to be restored with manifold interest and eternal life granted besides. Gill answers the same expectation without naming it, denying that more houses or parents or brethren are meant and putting in their place a comfort and peace and satisfaction not to be found in such enjoyments at all. Barnes adds only the older texts that stand behind the promise.
31:
Why the warning is given is answered alike by several. Gregory says the Saviour foresaw that his disciples' hearts would be troubled at the Passion and told them beforehand both the suffering and the glory of the rising. Chrysostom adds the reason for the privacy, that it was not fitting to publish the word to the crowds lest they be troubled, while the disciples, made familiar with it by expectation, might bear it better. Cyril states a second purpose, to convince them that he foreknew what was coming and went to it of his own accord, so that they might never say that one who promised them salvation had fallen into enemy hands; and he grants that they did not yet know what the prophets had foretold, their understanding being opened only after the rising. Henry marks what is peculiar here, that the sufferings are set out as the fulfilling of the scriptures, by which consideration Christ reconciled himself to them and would reconcile the disciples; Robertson notes that the phrase may attach either to what was written or to what shall be accomplished. Wesley refers the reader to the parallels.

Lightfoot alone reconstructs the journey, joining this to the summons to go into Judea again, where the disciples had objected that their Master had lately been in danger, and describing them following him wondering and afraid; only the visit to the sick friend had been named at the outset, and the progress to Jerusalem was foretold on the way. He places the party at the ford beyond Jordan when the message about the sickness arrived.

The third day draws the sharpest exchange. Isidore of Pelusium marvels at the folly of those who ask how Christ rose before the three days were out: rising later than promised would have been a mark of weakness, rising sooner is a token of the highest power, as a debtor who promised payment after three days and paid on the day itself is admired rather than blamed. He then adds that the promise was not to rise after three days but on the third day. Robertson records the same variation without alarm, since one Gospel has the third day and another after three days in the same sense. Clarke goes back to a prophet's words, which he would render that on the third day God will raise him up and we shall live before him, so that the resurrection is at once pledge and cause of ours. Ellicott notices that one word in the list of indignities is peculiar to this Gospel.

Their failure is explained two ways. Gill says not one of them could take it in, since they could not reconcile it with their notions of the Messiah's temporal grandeur, which shows how little they knew of the prophecies. Barnes and Clarke agree, the one that they looked for a temporal prince and could not see how this consisted with prophecy, the other that they could not conceive how a Master of unlimited power would let himself be tormented and slain. Calvin is harsher, calling it stupidity not to understand a plain saying on a matter they had themselves suspected, and tracing it to the expectation of a prosperous advancement which made a shameful death seem absurd, from which he infers how madly a false imagination can seize the mind. Ellicott and Robertson attend to how the failure is described. Robertson counts three statements of it in one sentence, an imperfect of continued not-perceiving, a summary aorist and a past perfect for a settled state, and says it is no wonder the writer tries three times. Ellicott takes the verse as peculiar to this Gospel and as the analysis a physician would make, dwelling on the psychology that would later explain the disciples' bewilderment and their slowness to believe the rising: they heard the words without taking in the meaning.
35:
Two of the fathers explain why a miracle follows the prediction. Gregory says the disciples, being yet carnal, could not receive the words of mystery and are brought to a work they can see, a blind man given sight that a divine act might strengthen their faith. Theophylact draws another lesson from the placing, that our Lord did not so much as walk without doing good, leaving his disciples the example that we should be profitable in everything and nothing in us be in vain. Pseudo-Chrysostom describes the moment: the man did not know him but felt a drawing towards him and grasped with his heart what his sight could not embrace, so that when those who could see told him only that Jesus of Nazareth was passing, he was told one thing and proclaimed another.

The account will not fit the others without work, and all notice it. Ellicott states it exactly: this Gospel agrees with the second and not the first in giving one blind man rather than two and in placing the cure on the approach to Jericho rather than the departure, and it passes over the request of the two brothers. Henry reports the same divergence, one evangelist naming a single man cured on the way out, another giving two. Robertson offers a topographical solution in the two Jerichos, the old and the new Roman town, with the beggar sitting by the road between them; the name is supplied by the second Gospel and the second man by the first. Clarke names him and refers the reader elsewhere, as Barnes and Wesley do. Augustine solves it allegorically: taking the town to signify the moon and so death, he has our Lord approaching his death command the Gospel preached to the Jews only, signified by the one blind man here, and after rising and ascending to Jews and Gentiles both, signified by the two in the other Gospel.

What the man's cry contains is pressed by two very different readers. Cyril observes that a man brought up a Jew would know that God was to be born of David's seed according to the flesh, and so addresses him as God while calling him son of David; he wishes those who divide Christ in two would imitate him, and notes that checks put on his confession did not damp his ardour. Gill says the same more plainly, that he believed him at once to be the Messiah, son of David being a well-known title; Robertson agrees that the address shows a recognition of the Messiah. Ambrose reads the man as a figure, the Gentile people receiving back through the sacrament of our Lord the brightness of the light they had lost, and finds it no difficulty that one Gospel has two, the Gentiles descending from two sons of Noah and so putting forward two authors of their race.

The small words are weighed at the close. Ellicott notes that the crowd is heard without an article, which better renders the vague impression left on a blind man by many footsteps and voices, and that those who told him to be quiet were in advance of the company and probably not the disciples; on the healing word he prefers made whole to saved, hearing behind it the spiritual sight of which the bodily cure was type and earnest. Robertson marks that the stopping is expressed by a different form here, and that the following at the end may be either a beginning or a continuing. Clarke ends on the crowd's praise, that they saw the finger of God while the Pharisees would not, and remarks that common people are often better judges of the work of God than the learned, being simpler and less warped by prejudice or self-interest.
